newsitem.title: PHILIPPINES: Manila's SEC vows to be tough on insider trading.
newsitem.headline: Manila's SEC vows to be tough on insider trading.

text.p: Philippines' regulators will shortly submit to Congress a list of firms which according to a probe by the Philippine Stock Exchange may have violated insider trading rules.
Securities and Exchange Commission chairman Perfecto Yasay told Reuters in an interview on Friday the list included 30 to 50 firms investigated since 1995.

"We will submit a list of the cases being investigated by the Philippine Stock Exchange ... we are not at liberty to disclose the details." Yasay said, adding that the list would be submitted to the House Committee on Banks and Financial Intermediaries.
Yasay said the SEC had decided to submit the list to the legislature because the House Committee had asked for it.
He did not say when the list would be submitted to Congress but said it would be as soon as possible.
In investigations by Congress in the past, legislators held public hearings before recommending either adoption of tougher measures or prosecution.
The revelation of the number of firms on the list surprised the market.

Helen Alvarez, vice-president at All Asia Securities, said, "30 to 50 brokers, that's big. It's not very encouraging for foreign investors especially. Honestly, the issue should be settled once and for all even if it will be a long and tedious process."
Roman Azanza, director at Crosby-UBP Securities Inc, said the probe would be futile if it did not produce results.
"There must be something wrong if after a long time, there's no prosecution," he said.
The Philippines made insider trading a crime under a Revised Securities Act it passed in 1981 but there has not been a single prosecution.
Market speculation of disputes within the bourse over the pace of reforms heightened last week when several senior officials, including president Vitaliano Nanagas, resigned.
Members of the bourse's governing board said Nanagas had to leave because his management style had angered staff.
Nanagas said his aim was to make the bourse more professional and said that he "may have moved too fast".

Asked whether the investigations would affect the Philippine Stock Exchange's bid for permanent self-regulatory organisation (SRO) status, Yasay said: "Yes, we also want to find out how the PSE would be able to efficiently respond to these types of situations."

"We want to know if the investigations conducted are thorough and if the sanctions imposed, if any, are adequate. Under the concept of the SRO, the PSE must maintain a high degree of independence that will allow it to police and discipline its membership," he said.
Last December, the SEC granted temporary SRO status to the PSE but the permit expired on February 28.
